AL: Registration plates became mandatory in Alabama on October 1, 1911.

Mercedes-Benz built its first passenger car plant outside Germany at Vance, with production starting in 1997.
Guinness lists the Barber museum in Leeds as the world's largest motorcycle museum.
AK: Territorial Alaska began issuing license plates to all motor vehicles in 1921.
Wartime metal rationing put Alaska drivers on fiberboard plates from 1945 to 1948.

Cars and trains share one lane inside the 2.5-mile Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel to Whittier.

AZ: The first state-issued Arizona plates went out on January 1, 1914.

London Bridge was shipped from England and rededicated at Lake Havasu City in October 1971.

AR: Motor vehicle plates were first required in Arkansas in March 1911.
Land of Opportunity ran on Arkansas plates from 1950 until the 1980s.

Highway 7, running north through the Ozarks, became Arkansas's first designated scenic byway in 1993.
CA: California began issuing its own plates in 1914; before that drivers supplied their own.

Gold lettering on black was the standard California plate look from 1963 to 1969.
The Arroyo Seco Parkway, opened to Pasadena in 1940, was the first freeway in the western states.
A San Luis Obispo lodging house coined the word motel when it opened in December 1925.
From its 1937 opening until 1964, the Golden Gate Bridge had the longest suspension span anywhere.
CO: Registration plates arrived in Colorado in July 1913.
A mountain range has been the standard Colorado plate design since 1960, with a few years off.

Trail Ridge Road tops out at 12,183 feet, the highest continuous paved road in the United States.
US 550 between Ouray and Silverton, the Million Dollar Highway, runs cliffside without guardrails.
CT: Connecticut drivers registered cars from 1903 but supplied their own plates until the state issued them in 1905.

Hartford's Pope Manufacturing showed off its Columbia electric carriage in May 1897.
The Heroes Tunnel, cut through West Rock at New Haven in 1949, was Connecticut's first road tunnel.
DE: Delaware plates have been numbered straight up from 1 since 1910, and low digits are prized.

Any Delaware plate issued since 1942 can still go on a car with a current sticker.
Only a rear plate has been required in Delaware since 1945.
The twin spans of the Delaware Memorial Bridge opened in 1951 and 1968.
Dover's one-mile oval, nicknamed the Monster Mile, has been paved in concrete since 1995.
FL: Florida was the last of the lower 48 to issue license plates, waiting until 1918.

GA: Georgia's 1941 plate was the first reflective general issue in the country.

Savannah's public roads hosted the American Grand Prize race in November 1908.
A traffic reporter called Atlanta's five-level I-85 and I-285 interchange Spaghetti Junction in 1986.
HI: Hawaii's counties issued their own plates from 1906 until a statewide design arrived in 1922.

A rainbow has been screened across the standard Hawaii plate since 1991.

The Hana Highway on Maui packs in 620 curves and 59 bridges, 46 of them one lane wide.
Roadside billboards were outlawed in Hawaii in 1927, decades before statehood.
ID: Idaho started issuing license plates in May 1913.
The 1928 Idaho plate carried a large potato, one of the earliest pictures on an American plate.
Famous Potatoes has run along the bottom of Idaho plates since 1957.
The Perrine Bridge at Twin Falls is the one US structure open to BASE jumpers year round.
Evel Knievel's steam rocket failed to clear the Snake River Canyon on September 8, 1974.
Apollo astronauts studied volcanic rock at Craters of the Moon in Idaho in 1969.
IL: Illinois required registration in 1907 but did not issue plates itself until 1911.
Land of Lincoln has been on Illinois plates since 1954.

IN: Drivers here supplied their own plates until the state began issuing them on July 1, 1913.

Auburn keeps a museum of Auburn, Cord and Duesenberg cars in the old factory's office building.
IA: For three years starting in 1953, Iowa plates read The Corn State instead of the usual Hawkeye State.

Madison County still has six covered bridges built between 1868 and 1889.
KS: Kansas plates read The Wheat State from 1949 until 1975.

A marker on I-70 west of Topeka claims the first stretch of Interstate finished under the 1956 act.

A stone monument near Lebanon marks the geographic center of the 48 contiguous states.
Cawker City's roadside ball of sisal twine weighs more than ten tons and keeps growing.
KY: The 1927 Kentucky plate was the first US passenger plate to name the county that issued it.

The Cumberland Gap Tunnel, opened in 1996, carries US 25E for 4,600 feet under the mountain.
Bluegrass State has appeared on standard plates since 1988.
Mammoth Cave, the longest known cave system on Earth, lies west of Interstate 65.
LA: For one year, 1954, Louisiana plates advertised yams.

The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway runs nearly 24 miles, the longest continuous bridge over water.
Interstate 10 crosses the Atchafalaya Basin on an 18-mile pair of bridges opened in 1973.
Streetcars have run on the St. Charles line in New Orleans since 1835.

ME: Vacationland has appeared on Maine plates since 1936.

The Maine Turnpike opened in 1947 as the second toll superhighway in the country.

A paved road 3.5 miles long climbs Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park.
MD: Construction of the National Road began at Cumberland in 1811 using federal money.

Maryland began issuing its own plates in 1910, six years after registration became law.
Plates in 1934 carried the word Tercentenary for the colony's 300th anniversary.
MA: The first license plates in the country were issued here on September 1, 1903.

MI: The world's first mile of concrete highway was laid on Woodward Avenue in Detroit in 1909.

MN: 10,000 Lakes has been printed on Minnesota plates since 1950.

MS: Registration and plates were required in Mississippi starting June 1, 1912.

The Natchez Trace Parkway runs 444 miles from Natchez to Nashville, Tennessee.
US Highway 61 through the Delta is known as the Blues Highway.
Elvis Presley was born in a two-room house in Tupelo in 1935, and the house still stands.
MO: Show-Me State has been on Missouri plates since 1979.

The Chain of Rocks Bridge over the Mississippi has a 22-degree bend in the middle.

MT: Numbers 1 to 56 on Montana plates stand for counties, ranked by their 1930 populations.

NE: Nebraska plates have carried a county number since 1922, ranked by how many cars each county had.

NV: Inmates made Nevada's plates at the Nevada State Prison from 1928 until the work moved in 2012.

NH: Live Free or Die reached ordinary New Hampshire passenger plates in 1971.

NJ: A 1949 law still keeps New Jersey drivers from pumping their own gasoline.

The Holland Tunnel opened under the Hudson in 1927, its fans replacing the air every 90 seconds.
Jughandle ramps send New Jersey drivers to the right so they can then turn left across the road.

NM: New Mexico prints USA on its plates so nobody mistakes the state for the country to the south.

NY: New York became the first state to require car registration, in 1901, using the owner's initials.

NC: First in Flight has topped standard North Carolina plates since 1982.

ND: Peace Garden State has ridden along on North Dakota plates since 1956.
Discover the Spirit served as the plate slogan from 1993 until late 2015.

OK: The world's first parking meter went up in Oklahoma City on July 16, 1935, at a nickel an hour.

A 66-foot steel soda bottle has lit up Route 66 at Arcadia since 2007.
OR: Oregon enacted the country's first gasoline tax in 1919, at one cent per gallon.

PA: The Pennsylvania Turnpike opened on October 1, 1940, and is often called the first superhighway.

RI: Ocean State has appeared on Rhode Island plates since 1972.

WI: America's Dairyland has been printed on Wisconsin plates since 1940.

DC: The District did not issue its own plates until October 1, 1907.

PR: Puerto Rico has required vehicle registration since 1906.

ON: Ontario drivers had to supply their own plates from 1903 until the province began issuing them in 1911.

SK: Land of Living Skies has been on Saskatchewan plates since 1998.

NS: Canada's Ocean Playground has run along the bottom of Nova Scotia plates since 1972.

NB: New Brunswick plates read Picture Province from 1958 until 1977.

NT: Northwest Territories plates have been cut in the shape of a polar bear since 1970.

NU: Nunavut kept the bear-shaped plate when it separated from the Northwest Territories in 1999.
